article_text:
A meeting at TIFFCOM in 2023 brought Italian co-producers to “ The Violinist ,” the animated feature that went on to win the top prize at France’s Annecy International Animation Film Festival this year, Singaporean filmmaker Ervin Han told a panel at the Tokyo market.

Han, co-founder and CEO of Singapore’s Robot Playground Media, spoke at “Anime’s New Frontier: Structuring & Financing International Co-Productions,” a session at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival . Speakers agreed that international anime co-productions work best when overseas partners are involved early, with financing, deal structures and rights management considered from development through release. Kawano Masao, program manager at Into Global, moderated.

Related Stories

Han co-directed and produced “The Violinist.” On his first TIFFCOM visit, he met Italian producer Cristiano Bortone and his team at Altri Occhi, who later joined the film as co-producers. This year, Han returned as producer to pitch “A Banquet for Hungry Ghosts,” an animated feature about food, horror and temptation, with partners from Singapore, Taiwan, Malaysia and Ireland.

Han described “The Violinist” as a story of friendship over a decade. The film itself also took 10 years from conception to completion. “With different roles in my projects, I find promotion is even more challenging than production,” he said.

Ilan Urroz, CEO of France’s Foliascope, said co-production itself was nothing new and stressed the importance of platform partnerships, pointing to France’s investment obligations for streaming services. Under French rules, streamers must put at least 20% of the revenue they earn in France into European or French-language original film and audiovisual production, rising to 25% for some services that offer films within 12 months of their theatrical release. The rule applies to animation as well as other genres. Urroz named Netflix, Disney+, Crunchyroll, Prime Video and HBO Max as the leading platforms in France.

Sakurai Taiki, CEO of Salamander Inc., drew on more than 25 years in anime and over 100 titles to stress the importance of people and talent. “Partners are the key to success,” he said.

Asked how to find co-production partners, Urroz said, “Be creative, and don’t forget that every project is also a journey of a group of people.”

editorial_title_zh: 影评 | 《街头霸王》（2026）：迷失了战斗的视线
editorial_excerpt_zh: 基陶·樱井将一群辨识度极高的格斗家搬上银幕，但剧本的分支与剪辑却削弱了看他们大显身手的乐趣。文章《影评 | 《街头霸王》（2026）：迷失了战斗的视线》首先出现在 Cinema com Rapadura 。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "基陶·樱井将一群辨识度极高的格斗家搬上银幕，但剧本的分支与剪辑却削弱了看他们大显身手的乐趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "要拍好一部《街头霸王》的改编作品，除了服装造型外，还需要认可每个角色独一无二的个性——无论是在空间中占据位置的方式，还是接近对手并施展招数的手法。由基陶·樱井执导的这部全新银幕作品在这些角色的外表上下足了功夫，却不断妨碍观众跟随他们投入动作场面。被缩短的搏击场面和那些与主角们争夺注意力的剪辑，让这部电影陷入了困境：它押注于一个格斗家的世界，却没能让格斗本身成为其最大的吸引力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在赢得一场世界锦标赛后，隆（安德鲁·浩二饰）接触到了一股邪恶的力量，这激起了反派豪鬼（乔·阿诺阿伊饰）的兴趣。多年后，同样企图利用这股力量的M·拜森（大卫·达斯马齐安饰）组织了一场新的比赛，旨在吸引自那以后便销声匿迹的隆。潜伏其中意图向独裁者复仇的春丽（Callina Liang饰）则被委派去集结各位格斗家。在这这一切的中间，还有隆和肯（诺亚·琴蒂内奥饰）之间那段原本应为重逢赋予个人维度的破裂关系。然而，剧本将注意力分散在如此众多的威胁和副线计划上，以至于锦标赛很快就失去了指引这场冒险的作用。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本片的剧情本可以组织得相对简单一些。这毕竟是一部格斗游戏改编电影，靠。没有什么比利用对决本身来确立宿敌关系并赋予胜利重要性更好的方法了。然而取而代之的是，绑架、家族冲突甚至中央情报局（！）的干预，在从未创造出同等吸引力的情况下打断了叙事。诸如古烈（科迪·罗德斯饰）、达尔锡（维尤特·杰姆瓦尔饰）、巴洛克（奥维尔·佩克饰）、拜伦（50 Cent饰）、嘉米（梅尔·詹森）和本田（后藤洋央纪饰）等配角的角色塑造虽然很容易被辨认出来，但却没有足够的空间，让观众对他们在片中的行为所产生的兴趣超越单纯认出他们的乐趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "强烈的色彩和电子音乐与演员们的表现相契合，所有这一切都试图找回90年代街机厅那种喧闹感——在那个时期，各种刺激因素争夺着站在机器前的人的注意力。樱井接受了这种夸张，并找到了与原作相匹配的呈现方式，而无需显得保守或貌似合理。然而，剪辑和中断接连不断，致使这种强度很难产生太多的变化。当一切似乎每时每刻都在要求同样的注意力时，这种对娱乐的邀请最终变得令人疲惫。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "片中呈现的第一场对决直接从第二回合开始，而有些交锋则在画外解决，只留给观众关于结果的信息。时间跳跃可以加快叙事节奏，但在这里它恰恰抹杀了支持观众观看锦标赛的那部分体验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "即使是在对决保留在镜头中的时候，剪辑的碎片化也让人难以跟进其演变过程。春丽对阵拜森的战斗以及隆对阵豪鬼和本田的交锋中，都有一些有趣的时刻。然而，这些对空间运用得当的微光，并不能保证动作戏的激动人心。这个问题甚至严重到了决战画面几乎让人看不到对肯的职业生涯如此决定性的一招。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "动画片段让这种局限性变得更加明显。这种技术以动作动画片特有的语言重现了隆和肯的过去。对决的速度和能量的爆发增强了角色的表现力。夸张感融入了动作之中，赋予了招式真人动作序列根本无法企及的强度。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部长片还包含一些愚蠢的对话和漫画式的反应，确立了一种能够容纳那个世界荒诞性的基调。并不是说夸张是优秀改编作品的唯一可行途径，但在所呈现的内容框架内它是合情合理的。然而，许多场景似乎笃信：仅仅出现一个古怪的角色本身就已经是个笑话了。当笑料没有奏效时，剩下的就是耗费时间去不断强调它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从幽默到隆和肯之间的戏剧性的过渡同样没有得到充分开发。这种羁绊虽然被呈现为情感核心，但在其他剧情的交织中却受到了断断续续的关注。表演之间的表现风格存在显着差异，浩二明显更加克制，而琴蒂内奥则表现出常常过火的外向。这虽然带来了一些幽默片段，但由于缺乏对关系的深入开发，导致戏剧性段落除了打断闹剧之外没有起到任何其他效果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《街头霸王》集结了合适的演员阵容以及能激起观众追随这些角色欲望的角色塑造工作。其最精彩的动画片段甚至展示了风格化如何能让对决更加激烈。然而，这部作品在支线岔路上耗费了太多时间，却剪掉了最核心的部分。这留下了一种遗憾：把格斗家们带到观众面前，却又一次次让战斗淡出视野。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Kitao Sakurai leva às telas um elenco de lutadores reconhecíveis, mas os desvios do roteiro e a montagem comprometem o prazer de vê-los em ação."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fazer uma boa adaptação de “ Street Fighter ” envolve reconhecer, além do figurino, a personalidade única de cada personagem, na maneira de ocupar o espaço ou até mesmo de se aproximar do adversário e executar um golpe. A nova incursão nos cinemas, dirigida por Kitao Sakurai, demonstra cuidado com a aparência desses personagens, mas atrapalha constantemente a possibilidade de acompanhá-los em ação. Os combates abreviados e a montagem que disputa a atenção com os próprios protagonistas comprometem um filme que aposta em um universo de lutadores sem conseguir fazer das lutas sua principal atração."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Após vencer um torneio mundial, Ryu (Andrew Koji) entra em contato com um poder maligno que desperta o interesse do vilão Akuma (Joe Anoaʻi). Anos mais tarde, M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), que também deseja se aproveitar desse poder, organiza uma nova competição visando atrair Ryu, que desde então está sumido. Chun-Li (Callina Liang), infiltrada em busca de vingança contra o ditador, é incumbida de reunir os lutadores. E no meio de tudo isso, há ainda a relação desgastada entre Ryu e Ken (Noah Centineo), que deveria dar uma dimensão pessoal ao reencontro. O roteiro, contudo, distribui sua atenção entre tantas ameaças e planos paralelos que o torneio rapidamente perde a função de nortear a aventura."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A trama poderia ser organizada com relativa simplicidade. É uma adaptação de um jogo de luta, carai. Nada melhor que usar os próprios confrontos para estabelecer as rivalidades e dar importância para as vitórias. Em vez disso, sequestros, conflitos familiares e até uma intervenção da CIA (!) interrompem a narrativa sem nunca criar um interesse equivalente. As caracterizações de personagens secundários como Guile (Cody Rhodes), Dhalsim (Vidyut Jammwal), Vega (Orville Peck), Balrog (50 Cent), Cammy (Mel Jarnson) e E. Honda (Hirooki Goto) são facilmente reconhecíveis, mas não há espaço o bastante para que o interesse pelo que fazem no filme supere o simples prazer de identificá-los."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As cores intensas e a música eletrônica se alinham ao comportamento do elenco, e tudo isso busca recuperar algo da agitação noventista dos fliperamas, onde diferentes estímulos competiam pela atenção de quem estava diante da máquina. Sakurai assume o exagero e encontra uma apresentação compatível com o material base, sem precisar parecer discreta ou plausível. Contudo, os cortes e as interrupções se sucedem sem que essa intensidade encontre muita variação. O convite à diversão acaba se tornando cansativo quando tudo parece exigir a mesma atenção o tempo todo."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "O primeiro combate apresentado já começa no segundo round, enquanto alguns enfrentamentos são resolvidos fora de quadro, deixando ao espectador apenas a informação sobre o resultado. Uma elipse pode acelerar uma narrativa, mas aqui elimina justamente parte da experiência que justificaria acompanhar o torneio."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mesmo quando os confrontos permanecem em cena, a fragmentação da montagem dificulta acompanhar sua evolução. Há momentos interessantes na luta de Chun-Li contra Bison e nos embates de Ryu contra Akuma e E. Honda. Esses lampejos de bom uso do espaço, porém, não garantem a empolgação das sequências. article_text:
Kitao Sakurai leva às telas um elenco de lutadores reconhecíveis, mas os desvios do roteiro e a montagem comprometem o prazer de vê-los em ação.

Fazer uma boa adaptação de “ Street Fighter ” envolve reconhecer, além do figurino, a personalidade única de cada personagem, na maneira de ocupar o espaço ou até mesmo de se aproximar do adversário e executar um golpe. A nova incursão nos cinemas, dirigida por Kitao Sakurai, demonstra cuidado com a aparência desses personagens, mas atrapalha constantemente a possibilidade de acompanhá-los em ação. Os combates abreviados e a montagem que disputa a atenção com os próprios protagonistas comprometem um filme que aposta em um universo de lutadores sem conseguir fazer das lutas sua principal atração.

Após vencer um torneio mundial, Ryu (Andrew Koji) entra em contato com um poder maligno que desperta o interesse do vilão Akuma (Joe Anoaʻi). Anos mais tarde, M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), que também deseja se aproveitar desse poder, organiza uma nova competição visando atrair Ryu, que desde então está sumido. Chun-Li (Callina Liang), infiltrada em busca de vingança contra o ditador, é incumbida de reunir os lutadores. E no meio de tudo isso, há ainda a relação desgastada entre Ryu e Ken (Noah Centineo), que deveria dar uma dimensão pessoal ao reencontro. O roteiro, contudo, distribui sua atenção entre tantas ameaças e planos paralelos que o torneio rapidamente perde a função de nortear a aventura.

A trama poderia ser organizada com relativa simplicidade. É uma adaptação de um jogo de luta, carai. Nada melhor que usar os próprios confrontos para estabelecer as rivalidades e dar importância para as vitórias. Em vez disso, sequestros, conflitos familiares e até uma intervenção da CIA (!) interrompem a narrativa sem nunca criar um interesse equivalente. As caracterizações de personagens secundários como Guile (Cody Rhodes), Dhalsim (Vidyut Jammwal), Vega (Orville Peck), Balrog (50 Cent), Cammy (Mel Jarnson) e E. Honda (Hirooki Goto) são facilmente reconhecíveis, mas não há espaço o bastante para que o interesse pelo que fazem no filme supere o simples prazer de identificá-los.

As cores intensas e a música eletrônica se alinham ao comportamento do elenco, e tudo isso busca recuperar algo da agitação noventista dos fliperamas, onde diferentes estímulos competiam pela atenção de quem estava diante da máquina. Sakurai assume o exagero e encontra uma apresentação compatível com o material base, sem precisar parecer discreta ou plausível. Contudo, os cortes e as interrupções se sucedem sem que essa intensidade encontre muita variação. O convite à diversão acaba se tornando cansativo quando tudo parece exigir a mesma atenção o tempo todo.

O primeiro combate apresentado já começa no segundo round, enquanto alguns enfrentamentos são resolvidos fora de quadro, deixando ao espectador apenas a informação sobre o resultado. Uma elipse pode acelerar uma narrativa, mas aqui elimina justamente parte da experiência que justificaria acompanhar o torneio.

Mesmo quando os confrontos permanecem em cena, a fragmentação da montagem dificulta acompanhar sua evolução. Há momentos interessantes na luta de Chun-Li contra Bison e nos embates de Ryu contra Akuma e E. Honda. Esses lampejos de bom uso do espaço, porém, não garantem a empolgação das sequências. O problema chega ao ponto de a luta final mal permitir ver um golpe tão decisivo para a trajetória de Ken.

As passagens em animação tornam essa limitação ainda mais evidente. A técnica recupera o passado de Ryu e Ken com uma linguagem típica dos animes de ação. A velocidade dos confrontos e as explosões de energia ampliam a expressão dos personagens. O exagero participa do movimento, dando aos golpes uma intensidade que as sequências com atores simplesmente não conseguem alcançar.

O longa conta ainda com diálogos bobos e reações caricatas, estabelecendo um tom que comporta os absurdos daquele universo. Não que a extravagância seja o único caminho possível para uma boa adaptação, mas faz sentido dentro do que foi apresentado. Muitas cenas, porém, parecem confiar que a simples presença de um personagem excêntrico já constitui uma piada. Quando a graça não acontece, sobra o tempo dedicado a insistir nela.

As passagens do humor para o drama entre Ryu e Ken também são pouco desenvolvidas. O vínculo é apresentado como centro emocional, mas recebe uma atenção descontínua em meio às outras tramas. A diferença de registro entre as atuações é discrepante, com Koji bem mais reservado e Centineo numa extroversão que constantemente passa do ponto. Isso rende sequências de humor, mas falta desenvolver a relação para que as passagens dramáticas tenham um efeito além de interromper a galhofa.

“Street Fighter” reúne um elenco adequado e um trabalho de caracterização que desperta vontade de acompanhar aqueles personagens. Seus melhores trechos de animação mostram, inclusive, como a estilização poderia tornar o confronto mais intenso. A obra, entretanto, ocupa tempo demais com desvios e corta aquilo que mais importava. Fica a frustração de colocar os lutadores diante do público e, repetidas vezes, tirar a luta de vista.

article_text:
Die Künstlerin Rosemarie Trockel ist mit dem Preis der Kulturstiftung Dortmund 2026 für ihr Lebenswerk ausgezeichnet worden

Der mit 25.000 Euro dotierte Ehrenpreis wurde am Donnerstag im Baukunstarchiv NRW in Dortmund verliehen. Trockel ließ sich bei der Preisverleihung von ihrer Galeristin Monika Sprüth vertreten. Das Preisgeld spendet sie zu gleichen Teilen an Frauenhäuser in Dortmund und Potsdam.

Die Laudatio hielt Yilmaz Dziewior, Direktor des Museum Ludwig in Köln und Mitglied der Fachjury. Er hob die Vielseitigkeit und Eigenständigkeit von Trockels Werk hervor, das sich seit mehr als vier Jahrzehnten eindeutigen Kategorien entziehe. Die Künstlerin verbinde unterschiedliche Materialien und Ausdrucksformen mit Humor und Widerständigkeit. Ihre Arbeiten hinterfragten gesellschaftliche Konventionen, kulturelle Zuschreibungen sowie das Verhältnis von Mensch, Tier und Technologie.

Im Rahmen der Preisverleihung wurde auch die Ausstellung "Déjà-vu" eröffnet, die Trockel eigens für das Baukunstarchiv NRW konzipiert hat. Sie versammelt Pigmentdrucke aus unterschiedlichen Schaffensphasen und beschäftigt sich unter anderem mit Wahrnehmung, Erinnerung, Identität und Geschlechterrollen. Auch den Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz thematisiert die Künstlerin in der Werkserie "Blind Mother". Die Ausstellung versteht sich nach Angaben der Veranstalter nicht als klassische Retrospektive, sondern als zeitgenössische Würdigung eines sich stetig weiterentwickelnden Werks. Sie ist bis zum 15. November zu sehen.

Der Preis der Kulturstiftung Dortmund wird seit 1998 vergeben und würdigt herausragende künstlerische Lebenswerke in den Bereichen Musik und Bildende Kunst. In der Sparte bildende Kunst wird er mit Trockel erstmals seit 2012 wieder verliehen. Zu den früheren Preisträgern zählen unter anderem Jörg Immendorff, Jürgen Partenheimer, Otto Piene und Heinz Mack.

article_text:
Nella pittura di Alberto Savinio , il corpo assume la struttura di un congegno, il mito genera configurazioni inattese, il giocattolo acquista la solennità del monumento. Le immagini incrinano le abitudini dello sguardo e rendono instabili le categorie con cui interpretiamo il reale. La retrospettiva Alberto Savinio. Souvenir , curata da Sarah Cosulich e Pietro Rigolo alla Pinacoteca Agnelli di Torino , riunisce oltre settanta opere e ricostruisce i principali nuclei di questa ricerca.

Il titolo introduce una riflessione sul ricordo come processo attivo. Il souvenir conserva una traccia dell’esperienza, affidandola al presente, dove assume significati ulteriori. Immagini familiari, miti e riferimenti alla cultura occidentale vengono selezionati e ricombinati, fino a generare rapporti inattesi. Il passato diventa così una materia capace di modificare la percezione del presente. Ricordare significa anche riconoscere in sé una componente divenuta estranea e scoprire possibilità rimaste in ombra. Da questa discontinuità nasce l’apertura all’alterità.

Il rapporto con Giorgio de Chirico , fratello di Savinio e figura centrale nello sviluppo pittorico della metafisica, aiuta a precisare la specificità della sua ricerca. Savinio rielabora anatomie, repertori mitologici e oggetti quotidiani, sottoponendoli a una continua riconfigurazione. L’enigma prende forma attraverso identità mobili, sospese tra familiarità e straniamento; la memoria culturale diventa uno strumento per interrogare il visibile.

In Le tendre quatuor (Hommage à Rapha ë l) (1928), quattro figure dalle tonalità rosa, azzurra, verde e viola occupano il primo piano. I corpi si articolano in volumi cilindrici e giunture quasi meccaniche; i volti, attraversati da reticoli geometrici, perdono individualità. Le pose oscillano tra abbandono e rigidità, mentre il paesaggio retrostante mantiene una profondità riconoscibile. Il richiamo a Raffaello evoca l’armonia classica mentre le anatomie ne alterano l’equilibrio organico. La tradizione diventa materia di trasformazione: il corpo si rivela una costruzione aperta a molteplici configurazioni.

In Bataille de Centaures (1930), la metamorfosi coinvolge il confine tra umano e animale. Le creature mitologiche si addensano in masse compatte, percorse da profili sinuosi e criniere mosse dal vento. La scena privilegia la presenza fisica dei centauri, sospesi tra anatomia umana e corpo equino. La loro natura ibrida rende permeabile una distinzione consolidata dalla cultura. Il mito riacquista così una forza critica: le immagini antiche tornano a interrogare le categorie con cui definiamo il vivente.

Con Monumento ai giocattoli (1930), l’indagine si sposta sugli oggetti. Sopra una base rocciosa si innalza una costruzione fantastica, composta da volumi geometrici, forme architettoniche ed elementi colorati. La verticalità richiama la monumentalità commemorativa, mentre i componenti rimandano alla libertà combinatoria del gioco. Gli oggetti si emancipano dalla funzione originaria e acquistano nuovi significati attraverso la disposizione reciproca. L’infanzia emerge come una forma di conoscenza fondata sulla possibilità di reinventare il mondo: il giocattolo diventa un’immagine autonoma, capace di sopravvivere al proprio uso.

Il percorso mette in relazione famiglia, mitologia, figure ibride, paesaggio e disegno. L’allestimento sobrio, con le opere distanziate sulle pareti grigie, favorisce l’osservazione e lascia allo spettatore il compito di stabilire connessioni tra i diversi nuclei. La pluralità degli interessi di Savinio – musicista, scrittore, drammaturgo e scenografo, oltre che pittore – si riflette in una concezione dell’immagine come luogo d’incontro tra linguaggi e forme di pensiero.

In Souvenir , la metamorfosi investe il modo stesso di concepire l’identità. Le forme custodiscono possibilità latenti e il ricordo ridefinisce continuamente il legame tra esperienza e presente. La pittura di Savinio sollecita uno sguardo disposto ad attraversare l’incertezza, riconoscendo in ogni figura una pluralità di esiti. La memoria diventa così un’esperienza di decentramento: il soggetto si confronta con ciò che lo eccede e trova nel passato l’innesco di nuove possibilità.

Il rilievo della retrospettiva risiede anche nella possibilità di restituire a Savinio una posizione centrale nel panorama artistico europeo del Novecento. La collaborazione con l’ Archivio Alberto Savinio, il contributo di un comitato scientifico internazionale e la riunione di opere provenienti da diverse collezioni sostengono una rilettura ampia della sua ricerca. Ne emerge la statura di un autore difficilmente circoscrivibile a una sola disciplina, capace di attraversare la cultura figurativa europea e di anticipare questioni che continuano a interrogare l’arte contemporanea.

article_text:
Die Diskussion um Raubkunst in der Sammlung Bührle sorgt im Kunsthaus Zürich weiterhin für Unruhe. Gerade haben die Zürcher Wähler für eine Aufstockung der öffentlichen Mittel gestimmt – doch die Zukunft ist alles andere als sicher

Ein sonniger Freitagnachmittag in einer ruhigen Seitenstraße in Zürich, Ende September. Auf der einen Straßenseite steht das modernistische Gebäude, in dem die Privatbank Rothschild untergebracht ist. Auf der anderen Seite, in der Einfahrt einer prunkvollen Villa aus dem 19. Jahrhundert, halb versteckt hinter einer großen Hecke, steht ein von dem Künstler Jeff Koons entworfener BMW in Sonderedition – einer von 99 Exemplaren, die jeweils 350.000 Dollar kosten. Ein Nummernschild hat er nicht.

Die dahinter liegende Villa, in der derzeit eine von einem lokalen Sammler organisierte Ausstellung über historische Schweizer Plakate zu sehen ist, beherbergte früher den Schatz an impressionistischen Meisterwerken der Bührle-Stiftung, der inzwischen ins Kunsthaus, Zürichs Pendant zu einer Nationalgalerie, umgezogen ist. Der Wagen, der mit der Ausstellung wenig zu tun zu haben scheint, ist die Leihgabe eines Plakatsammlers aus der Autobranche.

Diese Straßenszene fängt die Dynamik ein, die die Zürcher Kunstwelt prägt: private Interessen und enormer Reichtum, die sich im Zusammenspiel zwischen der Stadt, ihren Finanziers und Industriellen sowie ihren kulturellen Institutionen entfalten. Im Kunsthaus Zürich ist die Lage eskaliert. Die Stimmberechtigten haben gerade zugestimmt, mehr für den Betrieb eines Gebäudes zu zahlen, das um die Bührle-Kunstsammlung herum konzipiert wurde – eine Sammlung, die in acht Jahren möglicherweise nicht mehr da ist. Wem die Hauptattraktion des Museums gehört und wer für ihre dunkle Vergangenheit Rechenschaft ablegt, bleibt offen.

Größer, voller und tiefer in den roten Zahlen

Am 27. September stimmten die Zürcherinnen und Zürcher einer Erhöhung des jährlichen Beitrags der Stadt an das Kunsthaus, das größte Kunstmuseum der Schweiz, um 7,3 Millionen Schweizer Franken (7,7 Millionen Euro) auf 25,8 Millionen Franken (27,3 Millionen Euro) zu. Nur 55,4 Prozent stimmten mit Ja – ein weitaus knapperer Vorsprung als im Gemeinderat, dem Stadtparlament, der die Erhöhung mit 100 zu 16 Stimmen beschlossen hatte. Das Haushaltsdefizit war auf Kosten im Zusammenhang mit dem von David Chipperfield entworfenen, 2021 eröffneten Erweiterungsbau im Wert von 206 Millionen Franken (218 Millionen Euro) zurückzuführen: In den ursprünglichen Berechnungen waren dessen Betriebskosten unterschätzt worden.

Das größere Gebäude und das gestiegene Publikumsinteresse an der zugehörigen Sammlung haben sich nicht positiv auf das Geschäftsergebnis ausgewirkt . Die Besucherzahlen stiegen von rund 270.000 im Jahr 2019 – dem letzten vollständigen Jahr vor der Pandemie und vor der Eröffnung des Erweiterungsbaus – auf mehr als 500.000 pro Jahr. Dennoch hat das Museum seitdem jedes Jahr ein Defizit verzeichnet, zuletzt 1,53 Millionen Franken (1,61 Millionen Euro) im Jahr 2024 und 1,43 Millionen Franken (1,51 Millionen Euro) im Jahr 2025 – eine Zahl, die durch die einmaligen Erlöse aus einer Restitutionsvereinbarung verbessert wurde. Im Mai 2025 weigerte sich der Stadtrat, das Budget der Kunstgesellschaft ohne einen Plan zur Beendigung des anhaltenden Defizits zu genehmigen, was die Volksabstimmung nach sich zog.

Die Situation entwickelte sich zu einem Streitpunkt in der Presse und der Öffentlichkeit. Philipp Hildebrand, ehemaliger Präsident des Direktoriums der Schweizerischen Nationalbank, derzeitiger Vizevorsitzender von BlackRock und Präsident der Zürcher Kunstgesellschaft – des privaten Vereins, der das Museum betreibt –, erklärte gegenüber der Zeitung "NZZ" , er sei "kein Fan von Subventionen". Auf die Frage, ob die Kostensteigerung absehbar gewesen wäre, sagte er: "Diese Frage ist für mich nicht mehr relevant. Wir müssen nach vorne blicken." Die Direktorin des Kunsthauses, Ann Demeester, fasste sich kürzer: Das Museum sei "supersized" worden.

Für Bührle gebaut

Das Chipperfield-Gebäude wurde speziell für eine bestimmte Sammlung errichtet . Emil Georg Bührle (1890–1956), ein in Deutschland geborener Industrieller, verdiente sein Vermögen zwischen 1940 und 1944 mit dem Verkauf von Waffen an Nazideutschland und an das faschistische Regime Italiens – mit dem Segen der Schweizer Behörden.

Einen Großteil davon investierte er in Kunst, und das Ergebnis war eine der bedeutendsten Privatsammlungen Europas für französischen Impressionismus und Postimpressionismus. Zu den Höhepunkten zählen Paul Cézannes "Garçon au gilet rouge" (1888/90), Claude Monets "Le Bassin aux nymphéas, reflets verts" (1920), Auguste Renoirs "Irène Cahen d’Anvers" (1880), Vincent van Goghs "Le Semeur au soleil couchant" (1888) und Amedeo Modiglianis "Nu couché" (1916).

Nach dem Krieg musste Bührle 13 Raubkunstwerke zurückgeben; neun davon kaufte er den Eigentümern wieder ab. In den folgenden Jahrzehnten begann sein Geld, das Museum zu prägen: 1958, zwei Jahre nach seinem Tod, wurde ein von ihm finanzierter Flügel eröffnet. Im Februar 1960 gründeten seine Witwe Charlotte und ihre Kinder Dieter und Hortense eine Stiftung zur Verwaltung der Sammlung, die heute etwa 200 Werke umfasst. Die Werke zogen 2021 aus der Villa, welche die Sammlung beherbergte, in den Chipperfield-Bau um; die Leihgabe läuft bis Ende 2034 und kann verlängert werden.

Scheidungsgründe?

Die Partnerschaft zwischen dem Kunsthaus und der Bührle-Stiftung scheint sich verschlechtert zu haben. Ein Bericht aus dem Jahr 2024 unter der Leitung des Historikers Raphael Gross kam zu dem Ergebnis, dass die bisherige Provenienzforschung unzureichend gewesen war und dass "ein beträchtlicher Teil" der Werke vor dem Krieg in jüdischem Besitz war.

Gross bezeichnete die Sammlung als "historisch besonders belastet, in einem Ausmaß, das in der Schweiz möglicherweise einzigartig ist". Etwa 90 Werke müssen nun neu untersucht werden.

Die Stiftung nahm sechs Werke aus der Ausstellung, je eines von Monet, van Gogh, Courbet, Toulouse-Lautrec, Gauguin und Manet. Sie versprach "faire und gerechte Lösungen" mit den Erben. Zwei Fälle wurden inzwischen geregelt: Manets "La Sultane" (1871) und Gauguins "La route montante" (1884). In beiden Fällen sind die Bedingungen vertraulich, die Gemälde verbleiben in der Sammlung.

Eine "beispiellose mediale und politische Kontroverse"

Die Stadt investierte 88 Millionen Franken (93 Millionen Euro) in den Ausbau und verpflichtete sich mit der Abstimmung vom 27. September zu höheren Betriebskosten für ein Gebäude, das um eine Privatsammlung herum konzipiert wurde – eine Sammlung, deren Eigentümerin nun den Weg dafür geebnet hat, sie in acht Jahren an einen anderen Ort zu verlegen. Im vergangenen Jahr beantragte die Stiftung eine Änderung ihres Stiftungszwecks, damit die Sammlung nicht mehr an Zürich gebunden wäre und somit nach Ablauf des Leihvertrags den Standort verlassen könnte.

In dem Antrag wurde eine "beispiellose mediale und politische Kontroverse" angeführt. Man müsse prüfen, ob eine Fortsetzung der Zusammenarbeit mit dem Kunsthaus "noch möglich, angemessen und vertretbar" sei. Stiftungsrat Victor Schmid drückte es noch deutlicher aus: "Die Bilder gehören nur uns."

Im November 2025 erhob die Stadt Zürich beim Verwaltungsgericht Beschwerde gegen die Genehmigung der Zweckänderung durch die kantonale Stiftungsaufsicht. Sie argumentierte, sie sei "Destinatärin" der Stiftung, und verwies auf ihre Investition in den Ausbau. Bis Redaktionsschluss lag kein Urteil vor. Hildebrand betont dennoch, dass das Verhältnis zur Stiftung "ausgezeichnet" sei. Und Demeester erklärte gegenüber der "NZZ": "Ob Monets Wasserlilien dem Kunsthaus gehören oder als Dauerleihgabe bei uns hängen, ist dem normalen Besucher letztlich egal."

Die andere Hälfte

Als im Februar 1960 die Stiftung Sammlung E.G. Bührle gegründet wurde, wurde die Kunst aufgeteilt. Das von Lukas Gloor, dem früheren Direktor der Stiftung, zusammengestellte und 2017 veröffentlichte Inventar der Stiftung listet alle 633 Werke auf, die Emil Bührle erworben hatte, sowie die jeweiligen Verkäufer. Davon gingen 203 in den ständigen Bestand der Stiftung über, 26 wurden zum Verkauf bestimmt, um den Unterhalt der Stiftung zu finanzieren, 76 waren bereits verkauft oder getauscht worden, und 330 verblieben als "Privatsammlung" bei den Erben.

Von den neun Werken, die Bührle nach dem Urteil des Schweizerischen Bundesgerichts von 1948 von Paul Rosenberg, dem Nachlass Kann und Lévi de Benzion zurückkaufte – alle stammten 1942 und 1943 vom selben Luzerner Händler, Theodor Fischer –, gehören heute sieben der Stiftung. Die Werke mit der am besten dokumentierten Kriegsgeschichte hängen daher im Kunsthaus, wo die Öffentlichkeit nun für deren Erforschung aufkommt.

Doch der größere private Teil, für den es überhaupt kein Forschungsprogramm gibt, birgt noch offene Spuren: Am 21. März 1942 versteigerte Fischer die Sammlung von Julius Freund, einem jüdischen Berliner Sammler, der 1939 nach Großbritannien emigriert und 1941 dort verstorben war. Der von seiner Tochter, der Fotografin Gisèle Freund, organisierte Verkauf sollte seine verarmte Witwe Clara unterstützen .

Anteil "größtenteils verkauft"

Bührle erwarb 16 Lose. 14 blieben 1960 im Familienbesitz, und keines ging an die Stiftung. Im November 2025 einigte sich das Kunstmuseum Basel mit den Erben von Freund über acht Werke aus jener Auktion.

Der Anteil von Emil Bührles Sohn Dieter an der Privatsammlung sei später "größtenteils verkauft" worden, berichtete das Wirtschaftsmagazin "Bilanz" 2017. Der Bestand des Anda-Zweigs, also des Erbteils der Tochter Hortense, dessen Erben heute ihr Sohn Gratian Anda anführt, sei dagegen "nahezu unverändert geblieben", sagte Lukas Gloor, damals Direktor der Stiftung, dem Magazin. Ein Vertrauter der Familie bezifferte dessen Wert gegenüber "Bilanz" auf rund eine Milliarde Franken.

Am 11. Juli 2025 verzeichnete das Handelsregister, dass Anda und sein Cousin Carol Franz-Bührle nicht mehr dem Stiftungsrat angehören; damit sitzt dort kein Familienmitglied mehr. Fünf Wochen später, am 18. August, genehmigte die kantonale Stiftungsaufsicht den neuen Stiftungszweck, der die Bindung an Zürich streicht, vorbehaltlich der Beschwerde der Stadt. Die Familie Anda hat bis Redaktionsschluss nicht auf Fragen zur Privatsammlung, ihrer Provenienz und den Werken aus der Freund-Auktion geantwortet.

Wo das Gesetz aufhört

Das Inventar der Stiftung nennt die Verkäufer der Kunstwerke und deren Preise, nicht jedoch die früheren Eigentümer. Diese Lücke soll durch die eigenen Recherchen des Kunsthauses geschlossen werden. Die Stadt hat 3,86 Millionen Franken (4,09 Millionen Euro) bereitgestellt, die Kunstgesellschaft 2 Millionen Franken (2,12 Millionen Euro); der Kanton hatte für die Jahre 2023 bis 2026 bereits 700.000 Franken (740.000 Euro) gezahlt.

Laut "Swissinfo" befanden sich 133 der 205 an das Kunsthaus ausgeliehenen Werke vor 1945 zeitweise in jüdischem Besitz. Seit März 2026 arbeitet in der Schweiz die Expertenkommission für historisch belastetes Kulturerbe unter dem Vorsitz der ehemaligen Bundesrätin Simonetta Sommaruga.

Ihre Empfehlungen sind nicht bindend. Bei Fällen aus der Nazizeit kann eine Partei nur dann allein einen Antrag stellen, wenn sich das Werk im Besitz eines öffentlich finanzierten Museums oder einer öffentlich finanzierten Sammlung befindet; bei Werken in Privatbesitz müssen sich beide Seiten einig sein. Ob eine private Stiftung, deren Gemälde in einem subventionierten Museum hängen, unter diese Regelung fällt, ist noch nicht geklärt.

"Diese Zeiten sind vorbei"

Mit der Abstimmung vom 27. September wurde die Subvention für die Kunstgesellschaft bis Ende 2033 gesichert – ein Jahr vor Ablauf der Bührle-Leihgabe. Was danach geschieht, ist damit nicht geregelt, ebenso wenig wie der Verbleib der in Privatbesitz befindlichen Bührle-Werke, die von keinem öffentlichen Forschungsprogramm abgedeckt sind.

Auch die andere große private Leihgabe des Gebäudes ist nicht gesichert: Werner Merzbachers Sammlung von rund 65 Gemälden, die bis 2038 als Leihgabe zur Verfügung steht, ist in einen Streit zwischen seiner Familie und seiner Vermögensverwalterin, die er kurz vor seinem Tod als Erbin eingesetzt hatte, über seinen Nachlass verwickelt. "Historisch gesehen waren Museen ab dem späten 19. Jahrhundert unantastbare kulturelle Bastionen, ähnlich wie die Kirche", sagte Hildebrand gegenüber der "NZZ". "Diese Zeiten sind vorbei."

Die "Welt" hat genug von abstrakter Malerei, Festnahme nach Brandstiftung im Rathaus von Limoges, und Sotheby’s erprobt in Paris neue Wege: das ist unsere Medienschau am Dienstag

Museen CNN berichtet ein Jahr nach dem Louvre-Raub über den ehemaligen Kunstdieb Octave Durham , der heute dabei hilft, gestohlene Kunstwerke wiederzufinden. 2002 hatte Durham zwei Gemälde aus dem Van-Gogh-Museum in Amsterdam entwendet. Inzwischen arbeitet er mit dem niederländischen Kunstdetektiv Arthur Brand zusammen und nutzt seine Kontakte in die Unterwelt, um verschollene Werke aufzuspüren. Zugleich warnt der Beitrag vor einer neuen Welle von Museumseinbrüchen in Europa. Der Sicherheitsexperte Ibrahim Balut erklärt, dass Täter zunehmend mit schwerem Werkzeug vorgingen und oft in weniger als drei Minuten zuschlügen. Das Grundproblem liege im offenen Charakter von Museen: Sie sollen für Besucher zugänglich sein, während wertvolle Kunstwerke geschützt werden müssen. Durham würde dem Louvre gern bei der Sicherheit helfen: "Wenn sie mich fragen würden, würde ich ihnen zeigen, dass ich immer noch hineinkomme."

Kunstmarkt

Elisa Carollo beschreibt im "Observer" , wie Sotheby’s in Paris mit "Chez Sotheby’s" neue Wege im privaten Kunsthandel erprobt. In einer Wohnung an der Rue de Rivoli werden Werke im Wert von rund 150 Millionen Dollar präsentiert, darunter Arbeiten von Picasso, Matisse, Warhol und Gerhard Richter. Zum Konzept gehören auch ein Restaurant und eine Bar, die den Besuch zum Erlebnis machen sollen. Bereits bei der Vorbesichtigung seien sechs Werke verkauft gewesen. Valerio Polimeno, der das Projekt mit Sotheby’s entwickelt hat, versteht die Räume als lebendiges Wohnumfeld statt als klassische Ausstellung: Die Kunst solle sich in die Einrichtung einfügen und beiläufig entdeckt werden können. Sotheby’s reagiere damit auf die Nachfrage nach individuelleren Formen des Kunstkaufs. Während Auktionen weiterhin wichtig blieben, böten private Verkaufsausstellungen mehr Diskretion, Flexibilität und persönliche Betreuung.

Malerei

Hans-Joachim Müller kritisiert in der "Welt" die zunehmende Vereinheitlichung des internationalen Kunstbetriebs. Abstrakte Malerei , einst Ausdruck radikaler künstlerischer Freiheit, sei zur globalen Massenware geworden, und der Kunstbetrieb habe sich zu einer "gigantischen Designindustrie" entwickelt, in der sich ähnliche Malstile weltweit wiederholten. Statt eigenwilliger Positionen dominiere ein abstraktes "Massenbild", das sich in sozialen Medien als Meme verbreite. Die ursprüngliche Kraft der Moderne, neue Fantasieräume zu öffnen und das Publikum zu verstören, sei weitgehend erschöpft: "Die Kammern [sind] leer." Heute gehe es nicht mehr darum, "das nie Gesehene zu sehen", sondern um "die Vertrautheit mit dem immer wieder, immer neu Gesehenen". Selbst die versprochene Immersion sei zur vorhersehbaren Erlebnisroutine geworden. Zwar gebe es weiterhin herausragende Werke und Künstler, die ihren eigenen Weg gingen, doch würden sie von der Masse ähnlicher Angebote überlagert. Müller stellt deshalb die Frage, ob künstlerische Eigenwilligkeit überhaupt noch Voraussetzung für die Teilnahme am nächsten Galerienwochenende sei.

Kunstbetrieb

Auch Kunsthochschulen beteiligen sich an der französischen Protestbewegung von Schülerinnen, Schülern und Studierenden, berichtet "The Art Newspaper" .Sie fordern mehr Unterstützung für junge Menschen und warnen vor den Folgen politischer Instabilität und gekürzter Kulturetats. Jean-Baptiste Carobolante, Dozent an den Kunsthochschulen in Dunkerque und Tourcoing, erklärt, die Kultur sei häufig der erste Bereich, in dem gespart werde. Zugleich würden Kulturschaffende von reaktionären Politikern als politische Gegner behandelt: "Und warum sollte man politische Gegner finanzieren?" Ein Kunststudent bringt die Stimmung auf den Punkt: "Wir kämpfen für unsere Zukunft."

Kulturerbe

Nach dem Feuer im Rathaus der zentralfranzösischen Stadt Limoges während der landesweiten Ausschreitungen am Wochenende hat die Polizei nun einen mutmaßlich an der Brandstiftung beteiligten Mann gefasst. Spezialeinsatzkräfte hätten den Verdächtigen in einem Ort im Umland festgenommen, berichteten die Zeitung "Le Parisien" und der Sender CNews unter Verweis auf die Polizei. Demnach handelt es sich um einen polizeibekannten 40 Jahre alten Linksextremisten, der von den Behörden als sicherheitsrelevant erfasst ist. Nach Informationen des Senders RTL ist der Verdächtige den Ermittlern bereits wegen Gewalt gegen Amtsträger bekannt. In der Stadt mit rund 130.000 Einwohnern wurde das prächtige, unter Denkmalschutz stehende Rathaus am Samstag von Randalieren in Brand gesetzt und schwer beschädigt. Am Freitag wird Premierminister Sébastien Lecornu in Limoges erwartet. Am Rande landesweiter Demonstrationen gegen hohe Lebenshaltungskosten, an denen sich am Samstag hunderttausende Menschen zumeist friedlich beteiligt hatten, kam es zu schweren Ausschreitungen und Gewalt. Die Regierung schreibt diese vor allem Linksextremisten zu.

article_text:
Stephan James paid tribute to Carl Weathers by donning a white suit on Saturday at the AFI Fest screening of his new movie, “ I Play Rocky .”

James plays the late actor in the Peter Farrelly film, which chronicles the making of Sylvester Stallone’s “Rocky” in 1976. ”

“This is a three-piece custom King & Bay bespoke suit,” James told me while walking the red carpet at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. “My friends in Toronto at King & Bay remade this suit for me because Carl Weathers wore the exact same suit to the ‘Rocky II’ premiere in Philadelphia. It was a three-piece white suit, and I had them remake it so I can literally walk in his shoes yet again.”

The idea came from James’ publicist Samantha Hill. He accessorized with a rose brooch. “Carl had an actual rose, so this is my little twist on it,” James said. “I’m doing something a little more timeless with a brooch.”

Popular on Variety

Weathers played fighter Apollo Creed, who fought Rocky Balboa in the first two “Rocky” movies before becoming his coach in the third installment, and died in “Rocky IV” during a match against Ivan Drago (Dolph Lundgren). Weathers passed away in 2024 .

James also told me he had a little chat with Michael B. Jordan after he was cast as Weathers. Jordan played Apollo’s son in the three “Creed” movies. “‘Hey, I’m gonna be your daddy, Mike. I’m gonna be your daddy,’” James said. “So yeah, we had to talk.”

“I Play Rocky” stars Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone. The film has been earning critical raves — and Oscar buzz — since its premiere in early September at the Toronto International Film Festival.

The movie, from Amazon MGM, will be released in limited theaters on Nov. 6, followed by a wider release on Nov. 20.

article_text:
It’s late January, and the intrepid Film Comment crew has been on the ground reporting from an extra special edition of the Sundance Film Festival—the last to take place on the snowy slopes of Park City, Utah, the festival’s home since 1981, before moving to Boulder, Colorado in 2027. For the past week, we’ve gathered the best critics on the scene to talk about each day’s premieres on the Podcast.

For our final Podcast from Sundance 2026, critics Bilge Ebiri and Tim Grierson and programmer Madeline Whittle joined Film Comment Editor Devika Girish to close out the fest, discussing Padraic McKinley’s The Weight (2:56), Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York (24:26), Dawn Porter’s When a Witness Recants (28:46), Jason Osder and William Lafi Youmans’s Who Killed Alex Odeh? (34:34), Josephine Decker’s Chasing Summer (47:20), Walter Thompson-Hernández’s If I Go Will They Miss Me? (1:05:46), Hossein Keshavarz and Maryam Ataei The Friend’s House Is Here (1:10:28), Rafael Manuel’s Filipiñana (1:14:05), and more.

article_text:
“ Project Hail Mary ” was “the hardest movie” that Phil Lord and Chris Miller ever made — and they’re able to show their work. The filmmaking duo behind one of the year’s biggest hits built a deck to lead an audience through the challenging (but positive!) production process in a keynote presentation at IndieWire ‘s Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit presented by AT&T.

The one-hour presentation saw Lord and Miller dig into the behind-the-scenes process of the film ‘s production design evolution, stop-motion tests and how some of the story’s emotional highs came about through spontaneity.

“We wanted to make a movie about doing difficult things. And in order to do that, we had to make the movie as difficult as possible,” Lord said with a laugh.

“A movie about people coming together to accomplish something really hard,” Miller added. “This is what people have said to us about this movie.” The deck then revealed a slide reading, “You made me cry over a rock.”

“Hail Mary” stars Ryan Gosling as the sole survivor of an Earth-saving interstellar expedition. While he’s often the only human face on screen, Gosling gets quite the animated scene partner with Rocky, a fun-loving geode alien brought to life by a mixture of puppetry, computer-generated imagery, onstage vocal work and other production processes.

“We knew that we wanted to make him a physical puppet, at least to start. There’s a lot of CG in the movie, but we wanted the inspiration to be puppetry,” Lord said, presenting some stop-motion tests for the character. “I begged them to let us do the whole movie this way. It would have cost a billion dollars.”

“The movie lives and dies on their relationship,” Miller added. “The idea that Ryan could do the whole movie talking to a tennis ball on a stick by himself was impossible. We knew it had to be real scenes … The reason why you [watch ‘Star Wars’ and] believe Yoda — who’s kind of a shitty puppet — is because Mark Hamill believes it’s real and he confers authenticity onto it. Ryan really makes you believe because he has so much range and so much heart.”

Lord and Miller also broke down the origins of one of the film’s stand-out scenes: a flashback in which a usually stone-faced task force leader, played by Sandra Hüller, uncorks her own emotions with a karaoke performance of Harry Styles’ “Sign of the Times.”

“Ryan came to us and was like, ‘Sandra has an amazing singing voice. And she sings in between takes.’ And if you’ve ever saw the film ‘Toni Erdmann’ — if you haven’t, I recommend it — she sings and it’s fantastic,” Miller said.

“We concocted this idea that, instead of her staying apart from the karaoke thing to express how stoic and lonely she was, Ryan dares her to show her more human side that he can see,” Lord said. “The most uncool thing you can do to an actor is come to them 36 hours before and say, ‘Do you mind singing a song tomorrow?’ And she being a very gracious, incredible, delightful, super talented artist was like, ‘I’ll do it if I get to pick the song.'”

“Harry Styles! Really, really expensive song. That’s fine. That’s great,” Miller interjected jokingly.

“That should be easy to pay for and clear,” Lord said. “But you know what? Movie crews do impossible things.”

“We were able to get a clearance on it. We had no time to rehearse … And we didn’t tell the cast what she was going to sing,” Miller said. “The first thing we shot was the reaction of the cast, which is very genuine. We are very agog at how beautiful it was. And then we came around and shot Sandra’s side. And then our amazing editor — Joel Negron, who we’ve worked with for years — we ask them to cut it together like a dialog where she’s talking to the crew at first. And then by the end, she’s talking to Ryan directly.”

Watch Lord and Miller’s complete conversation in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. article_text:
There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II , the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “ The Mosquito Bowl ” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa.

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film , that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their plan of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

Perhaps that’s why the Mosquito Bowl itself only took up a single page of the Buzz Bissinger book on which Berg’s film is based, and why that source material used the game as a lens through which a light could be shined on the semi-forgotten men who found their way into the lineup that day. It’s been suggested that Bissinger played up the sports angle in order to capitalize on the success of his “Friday Night Lights,” and given that Berg adapted that book into a film as well, it stands to reason that his “Mosquito Bowl” should do the same.

The problem is that, in stark contrast to Bissinger, Berg and co-writer Mark L. Smith only seem to care about their characters as a means to an end. The project’s anti-war ethos is solely conveyed by reducing collegiate legends into cannon fodder, as the movie is considerably less interested in what bonds these boys together than it is in the shells that blast them apart.

Perhaps that explains why I’ve been able to write almost 650 words without bothering to mention any of their names. To the extent that it matters to a film so blandly de-saturated that everyone in it looks half-dead from the start, Nicholas Galitzine stars as Brown University legend John McLaughry — the only character we know for certain will survive the assault on Japan. (The movie opens with a sustained flash-forward of John staring longingly at an empty football field as “Friday Night Lights” veterans Explosions in the Sky layer their post-rock shimmer over the soundtrack). He’s got sad eyes, a square jaw, and a brunette girlfriend, which is more than you can say for Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), who has a devil-may-care attitude that disappears real quick once his unit makes land on Tawara. The only real source of contextual friction is owed to the rivalry between Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich (a glinty and magnetic Ray Nicholson) and the straight-laced mama’s boy he beat in a big game before the attack on Pearl Harbor (Tom Francis as the stoic and decent Dave Schreiner).

Individually, Butkovich is the only one of these characters who has the chutzpah to carry the movie on his back. Incidentally, he’s the only one of these men who was heading to the pros before the war got in the way. Still, it’s engaging to see them all blitz through life on their home turf, and “The Mosquito Bowl” benefits from Berg’s handheld and ruggedly naturalistic approach to how the players comport themselves off the field (read: they say “fuck” a lot and generally aspire to feel more like real people than they do patronizing impressions of what men were like in the ’40s).

But then the war comes to Hawaii, a match-cut turns a flock of birds into some fighter jets, and these beloved football stars all find themselves rendered nearly anonymous by the sea of shaved heads that are waiting for them at book. Little is made of their civilian celebrity, and even less of their individual decisions to enlist. “This is my rifle — there are many others like it, but this one is mine.”

Berg takes militaristic uniformity as all the excuse he needs to avoid deviating from expectation, and nearly everything that happens between basic training and the big game on the beach near Okinawa feels like it could have happened in several dozen other World War II movies, and almost certainly did. Defiant warriors curdle into terrified kids, bullets whizz through ocean waves, snipers pick off predictable characters at unsuspecting — or very suspecting — moments, and even the most hardened of marines find themselves staring blankly into the middle distance as their friends are decimated on all sides. Berg has always had a flair for the frenetic, and while there’s a perversely fetishistic veneer to the attention he devotes to entrails and enemy screams, it serves the film’s purposes that war has seldom seemed less survivable than it does here. (The film has no interest in humanizing the Japanese, but tries to compensate for that by presenting a few of the Americans as unrepentant monsters).

Still, for all of its supposed verisimilitude, “The Mosquito Bowl” seems less indebted to the reality of war than it does to Hollywood’s idea of it, and its abject refusal to flesh out its characters — a dereliction of duty, if ever there was one — makes it feel more contrived rather than less. I’m happy for Berg that he found a way to combine all of his favorite things into a single project (football, the military, and massive fireballs are all well-accounted for, even if Mark Wahlberg’s absence makes the whole movie feel like it’s forgotten something important), but “The Mosquito Bowl” accomplishes very little beyond violently illustrating that war is worse than football. It does that with such fervor that it loses all sight of what those things might really have in common.

Grade: C

Netflix will release “The Mosquito Bowl” in theaters on Friday, October 30. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, November 25.

Jesse Eisenberg’s “ The Debut ” snagged the top prize at the Middleburg Film Festival , which ran Oct. 15-18.

Starring Julianne Moore, Eisenberg’s third directorial outing won the audience award at the Virginia festival, which held its 14th edition over the weekend. Ava Duvernay’s “14th” took home the prize for best documentary feature, while “La Bola Negra” won best international feature.

“The Debut” opened this year’s festival, with a Q&A with Moore and Eisenberg following the screening. The film premiered at Telluride to best picture buzz, positioning Moore and co-star Paul Giamatti to be in Oscar conversations in the coming months.

Middleburg presented several tributes and honors over its four-day weekend. Léa Seydoux received the Outstanding Achievement in Acting Award for her role in “Gentle Monster.” Jordan Firstman received the Breakthrough Filmmaker Award for his feature directorial debut, “Club Kid,” which he wrote, directed and starred in.

Composer Daniel Pemberton was recognized with the Distinguished Composer Award for his work on “Project Hail Mary” and Danny Boyle’s “Ink.” Jack O’Connell received the Spotlight Actor Award for his performance as former tabloid editor Larry Lamb in the latter.

Olivia Colman attended the festival for both “Elsinore” and “Wicker.” “Elsinore” makeup and hair designer Nadia Stacey was presented with the Distinguished Makeup & Hair Design Award.

“The Odyssey” costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, production designer Ruth de Jong and editor Jennifer Lame received the Variety Creative Collaborators award . Variety ’s Jazz Tangcay moderated a conversation with the artisans on Oct. 16.

Following each screening, festivalgoers cast their vote for their favorite films. This year’s first runner-up was “Elsinore,” starring Andrew Scott and Colman, and second runner-up was “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich.

article_text:
London-based Radiance Films has acquired eight Taiwanese classics from the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute (TFAI), including works by acclaimed directors Hou Hsiao-hsien and Tsai Ming-liang , for theatrical and home entertainment releases in 2027.

The deal, unveiled at Lyon’s International Classic Film Market (MIFC) on Thursday, includes Hou’s “A Time to Live and a Time to Die” (1985) and “Dust in the Wind” (1986), alongside three films by Tsai: “ Rebels of the Neon God ” (1992), “Vive L’Amour” (1994) and “The River” (1997).

Also included are “In Our Time” (1982), a landmark anthology of the Taiwanese New Cinema movement, Chang Yi’s “Kuei-Mei, a Woman” (1985) and Yang Li-kuo ‘s “The Dull-Ice Flower” (1989). The latter will be released in both the U.K. and U.S., while the seven other titles are U.K.-only acquisitions.

Popular on Variety

Radiance plans individual releases and collections, including a Taiwanese New Wave set and a trio of Tsai films.

For Radiance founder Francesco Simeoni, the acquisitions are the culmination of years of efforts to secure films largely unavailable in Britain. After unsuccessful attempts to license titles from Taiwan’s Central Motion Picture Corporation, he finally established contact with TFAI at this year’s Berlin Film Festival. The deal took shape at Cannes, where he saw “The Dull-Ice Flower,” screened in Cannes Classics, and decided to include it in the package.

“Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang , I would argue, are among the most important filmmakers in world cinema ever,” Simeoni told Variety . “There are a lot of people who will be somewhat aware of them but not aware of where they started. I think it’s always important to understand where filmmakers come from.”

Radiance plans an extended theatrical rollout ahead of the home entertainment releases, beginning with screenings at London’s Garden Cinema later this month to build interest in the film, with further screenings and potentially streaming deals to follow.

Simeoni believes the films will resonate particularly with younger cinephiles, pointing to the enthusiastic response Radiance has received to comparable classics such as Noboru Nakamura’s “The Shape of Night” at theatrical screenings and film clubs, as well as through its online community. Much of that interest, he told Variety , appears to come from people in their twenties and thirties.

“There’s this group of people who are just starting on their cinephile journey and making discoveries for the first time first time and coming to us.”

The acquisitions come as restored film heritage finds new audiences and commercial opportunities through theatrical distribution, retrospectives and the collector-driven home entertainment market – a central theme at this year’s MIFC, where Taiwan received a spotlight .

At a panel titled “Taiwanese Cinematic Heritage: Preserving the Past, Shaping the Future,” TFAI chair Arthur Chu and programmer Howard Yang discussed the institute’s restoration and international distribution strategies alongside Radiance production manager Elena Lazic and Vincent Paul-Boncour, co-founder of French distributor Carlotta Films . The discussion was moderated by Taiwanese cinema specialist Wafa Ghermani.

TFAI has restored 110 titles since 2013 and now completes around a dozen restorations a year. Its early international strategy focused on acclaimed filmmakers, with 4K restorations of King Hu’s “Dragon Inn” and “A Touch of Zen” screening at Cannes Classics in 2014 and 2015. Now the institute is increasingly turning its attention to lesser-known films.

“These big-name, A-list filmmakers are like a springboard for us to engage with major festivals and markets, and connect with key players in the industry,” TFAI’s Chu said.

Audience demand also plays a role: a 2023 public survey identified “The Dull-Ice Flower” as one of Taiwan’s most popular classics, leading to its restoration and subsequent Cannes premiere.

Paul-Boncour pointed to Carlotta’s Edward Yang retrospective as an example of how restored classics can find renewed commercial life. In 2025, Carlotta brought Yang’s previously unreleased “A Confucian Confusion” and “Mahjong” to French theaters as part of a wider retrospective, followed by DVD and Blu-ray releases.

Again, the retrospective attracted a new generation of filmgoers, with Ghermani recalling long lines of young audiences waiting to attend screenings of Yang’s films.

For Paul-Boncour, the crucial step is ensuring that preservation leads to access. Restored films need more than festival exposure, he argued: they require distributors willing to invest in theatrical releases, promotion and home entertainment editions to give them a sustained commercial life.

But bringing such films back into circulation can be a lengthy and complicated process. Rights ownership, missing materials and music clearances remain significant obstacles, with negotiations sometimes stretching over years.

TFAI representatives acknowledged those challenges, particularly for older productions whose rights holders may be difficult to trace. The institute has also sought new partnerships with filmmakers, producers and sponsors to finance restorations and facilitate international distribution.

Beyond the commercial opportunities, the panel highlighted the cultural importance of Taiwan’s film heritage as the island marks the 70th anniversary of Taiwanese-language cinema.

More than 1,200 Taiwanese-language films were produced between the mid-1950s and late 1970s, but only around 200 are believed to survive. Often overshadowed by Mandarin-language productions promoted under Nationalist rule, these films offer a window onto Taiwanese society and identity long before the emergence of the New Wave.

“Especially due to the international geopolitical influence, I think Taiwan is increasingly gaining attention on the global stage,” said Chu. “This is the best way for us to promote our heritage through classic Taiwanese-language cinema.”

article_text:
The World Monuments Fund has raised $62 million for its endowment, beating its fundraising target 18 months ahead of schedule and giving the New York-based preservation organization considerably more financial muscle to protect historic sites around the world.

The campaign, announced Wednesday, has tripled the organization’s endowment net assets, which are expected to pass $100 million by 2028. The money will support everything from conservation training to emergency efforts to protect cultural heritage threatened by war, climate change, and natural disasters.

The fundraising drive was launched publicly less than a year ago as part of WMF’s 60th anniversary celebrations. It was built around a $20 million matching challenge from the Robert W. Wilson Charitable Trust, which pledged to match 50 cents for every dollar raised, up to $40 million in donations.

Other major contributors included philanthropist Suzanne Deal Booth , who gave $10 million toward a new institute for heritage preservation that bears her name, and Virginia James, whose contribution falls between $5 million and $10 million. The donor list also includes familiar art-world names such as Susan de Menil, Stephen Lash, Annabelle Selldorf , and Christian Louboutin.

“Cultural heritage is being lost to conflict, climate change, neglect, and urbanization faster than the world can respond,” Bénédicte de Montlaur, WMF’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “This campaign gives WMF the long-term resources to act with greater urgency and ambition.”

Founded in 1965, WMF has worked to preserve more than 700 sites across 114 countries. Its projects range from conserving historic buildings and archaeological sites to training local craftspeople and helping communities protect cultural landmarks after disasters.

The new funding will bolster several of those jobs. The Suzanne Deal Booth Institute for Heritage Preservation has secured $21 million in endowed funds to expand conservation training, research, and professional development. Another $1 million from the Donald A. Pels Charitable Trust will support WMF’s Crisis Response Program, which helps protect cultural heritage in the aftermath of war and natural disasters.

The organization has also raised $4 million for preservation projects in the field and established a $2 million endowed fund to support the World Monuments Watch, its biennial program identifying cultural heritage sites facing serious threats.

The fundraising success comes as WMF begins a new five-year strategic plan aimed at expanding its international reach and making historic preservation a greater global priority.

For an organization whose work often involves racing against time, whether to save a historic building from demolition or protect an archaeological site from conflict, the expanded endowment offers something particularly valuable: a more reliable source of funding for the years ahead.
